title: Optimized Financial Planning: Integrating Individual and Cooperative Budgeting Models with LLM Recommendations
authors: de Zarzà, I.; de Curtò, J.; Roig, G.; Calafate, C.T.
tldr: An optimization framework for individual and cooperative household budgeting integrates LLM recommendations as initial feasible solutions, combining econometric modeling with AI-driven insights to maximize savings.
problem_and_motivation: Individuals and households struggle with financial planning due to the complexity of modern economic systems and the limitations of traditional methods in personalizing recommendations. There is a gap in integrating real-time, AI-driven personalized recommendations into financial optimization models. The democratization of financial planning for non-experts remains an unaddressed challenge.
approach: Proposes a linear optimization model maximizing savings by allocating monthly income across expense categories with non-negativity and budget constraints.
Extends the individual model to a cooperative household model incorporating multiple incomes, shared expenses, and per-member preference weights.
Integrates GPT-4 LLM recommendations as initial feasible solutions and constraint bounds for the optimization framework.
Applies extended coevolutionary (EC) theory to model adaptive learning among household agents influenced by LLM outputs.
Introduces a RAG approach to mitigate LLM hallucination by grounding recommendations in verified financial data.
Validates using synthetic household datasets with normally distributed incomes and expenses across ten households.
findings: LLM-recommended savings plans align with established financial planning principles and produce economically sound allocations.
The combined LLM-plus-optimization approach yields higher savings than original unoptimized allocations across all synthetic households.
LLM suggestions include consumption smoothing, emergency funds, and retirement planning consistent with life-cycle hypothesis.
The cooperative model successfully accommodates individual preferences while maximizing collective household savings.
Qualitative comparison shows proposed LLM-integrated models outperform traditional methods in personalization, adaptability, and scalability.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper introduces a novel framework that bridges traditional econometric budgeting optimization with LLM-driven recommendations for both individual and household contexts. It extends cooperative game theory to household multi-agent systems where agents adaptively learn expense allocations influenced by AI suggestions. The integration of extended coevolutionary theory provides a theoretical foundation for how LLM outputs can guide iterative optimization. The work demonstrates feasibility through simulation with synthetic data, showing that LLM-informed optimization produces financially sound allocations aligned with established principles.
directly_justifies: LLM recommendations can serve as feasible initial solutions for budget optimization problems.
Cooperative household budgeting can be modeled as a multi-agent optimization with preference weights.
Extended coevolutionary theory provides a framework for adaptive financial learning with AI agents.
RAG methodology can mitigate LLM hallucination in financial recommendation contexts.
Combined LLM-plus-optimization outperforms unoptimized baseline allocations in savings.
limits: Simulation uses synthetic data only; no real-world household financial data validation.
LLM recommendations are not empirically evaluated against financial expert advice.
Utility function parameters are not empirically calibrated or validated.
Scalability to larger cooperative entities beyond households is untested.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned. Domain 7 (Budgeting Strategies and Optimization) is the primary focus, yielding codes 7.A, 7.B, and 7.C with high relevance. Domain 3 (Expense Categorization) is moderately relevant through 3.A given the use of standard expense categories. Domain 13 (Savings Goal Management) is relevant at 3.A due to savings maximization as the core objective. Domain 14 (Synthetic Data) is relevant at 3.A through the synthetic household data generation for simulation. Domain 4 (Landscape of Existing Systems) receives low relevance for its literature review of traditional and AI-driven tools. Domain 12 (Evaluation Frameworks) is low due to the qualitative-only comparison approach. Domain 5 (Financial Behavioral Profiles) is low as behavioral aspects are acknowledged but not formalized into profiles. Domains 1, 2, 6, 8, 9, 10, and 11 were considered and rejected as the paper does not address Filipino-specific demographics, culturally specific practices, predictive spending models, anomaly detection, mobile design, data privacy, or engagement mechanics.

limitations: Simulation uses only synthetic household data with no real-world validation.
LLM recommendations are not compared against human financial expert assessments.
Utility function parameters lack empirical calibration from real financial data.
Proposed RAG and verification mechanisms are not implemented or tested.
Scalability to larger entities beyond households remains unexplored.
